A septuagenarian is a person who is in their seventies — that is, someone who is at least 70 years old but has not yet reached their 80th birthday. If you know someone who is 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, or 79 years old, that person is a septuagenarian.

The exact boundaries: The word has very precise edges. A person becomes a septuagenarian the moment they turn 70. They stop being one the moment they turn 80. Not a day before, not a day after. So the word covers a strict ten-year window of a human life.

What the word does NOT mean: The word says nothing at all about the person's health, personality, energy level, wisdom, or lifestyle. A 76-year-old who runs marathons and a 76-year-old who rarely leaves the house are both, equally and without distinction, septuagenarians. The word is purely about age — nothing more.

The tone and register: Septuagenarian is a formal, slightly literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in a newspaper article, an official biography, a medical report, or a formal speech than in ordinary conversation. In casual speech, people typically just say "she's in her seventies" or "he's a seventy-something." In writing, however, septuagenarian adds both precision and a certain elegance. It tells you not just roughly how old someone is, but pinpoints exactly which decade of their life they are in.

• "The prize was awarded to a determined septuagenarian who had spent her seventies learning five new languages."
  • "At 74, the retired judge remained one of the sharpest septuagenarians in the legal community."
  • "The study followed a group of 200 septuagenarians over a period of five years."

Notice in each sentence that "septuagenarian" works just like any other noun referring to a person — it can be the subject of a sentence, the object, or used in a group/plural form.

Its place in a family of similar words: English has a neat, logical set of words that work exactly the same way for other decades of later life. Knowing the whole family makes the meaning of septuagenarian stick much better:

A sexagenarian is someone in their sixties (60–69). A septuagenarian is someone in their seventies (70–79). An octogenarian is someone in their eighties (80–89). A nonagenarian is someone in their nineties (90–99). A centenarian is someone who is 100 years old or older.

You can see the clean pattern: each word names a specific ten-year stretch of later life. Septuagenarian sits right in the middle of this family.

One small bonus note — adjective use: It is worth knowing that the very same word can also sit in front of another noun to describe it, functioning as an adjective. For example: "a septuagenarian athlete" or "septuagenarian voters." The word does not change its spelling or form when it does this. This is worth knowing so that you are not confused when you encounter it used that way in the wild.

The one-sentence summary to remember forever: A septuagenarian is simply any person who is aged between 70 and 79 years old — no more, no less.
